podcast.title: Birth and Origin
podcast.body: Born on October 7, 1968, in the small English town of Wellingboro. "He's from a tiny English town called Wellingboro. His birthday was October 7, 1968."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Childhood Nickname
podcast.body: Due to his pale and thin appearance at school, Tom was given the nickname "Salamander." This led to him getting into "a lot of fights," which even boxing lessons from his father couldn't significantly help. "he picked up the nickname Salamander."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: College Plans and Early Jobs
podcast.body: Before attending university, Tom decided to take a year off. During this time, he worked selling men's suits, a job he "hated." He then found a "better job" working in a mental hospital before eventually enrolling at Oxford. "Tom decided to take a year off before university. He spent some time selling men's suits, something that he hated. So he got a better job. It gave him a mental hospital before he went back and enrolled in Oxford."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Criticism of Streaming Services
podcast.body: Tom York is cited as one of the artists who "rage against the rise of streaming music services," indicating his strong opposition to this modern model of music distribution. "For example, guys like Tom York and David Byrne rage against the rise of streaming music services."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Bush: The Post-CD Band  Featuring Gavin Rossdale

podcast.title: DJ Gig at Campus Pub
podcast.body: To supplement his income, Tom worked as a DJ at a campus pub. He was quite skilled and his regular Friday night gigs often attracted "a thousand people or more" to hear him spin. "Tom supplemented his income working as a DJ at a campus pub. And he was pretty good too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Musical Frustration
podcast.body: Tom received his first guitar at the age of eight. However, he quickly became so frustrated with the instrument that he "smashed the thing to pieces in a big temper tantrum." "He got his first guitar at age eight, but he soon got so frustrated with it that he smashed the thing to pieces in a big temper tantrum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Band
podcast.body: After overcoming his initial frustration with the guitar, Tom formed his first band at age 10. "he eventually got his act together, and a few years later he formed his first band. This was age 10."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Guitar Hero
podcast.body: Tom York's earliest guitar hero was Brian May of Queen, whose guitar solo in "Bohemian Rhapsody" he still admires. "And his first guitar hero, it was Brian May of Queen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Meeting Stanley Donwood
podcast.body: While performing with The Headless Chickens in Exeter, Tom York met Stanley Donwood. Donwood went on to become, and remains, Radiohead's primary artist responsible for all their artwork and promotional materials. "it was while at Exeter, and playing in this band, that Tom met Stanley Donwood. He would go on to become a radio head's key guy when it came to artwork and promotional material."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Physical Characteristics and Health
podcast.body: Described as a "delicate little guy," standing approximately 5'5". He was often "sickly and skinny," which was a source of worry for his father, a chemical engineer and championship boxer. Tom was born with a partially paralyzed left eye, with the eyelid fixed in a downward position. After several surgeries intended to correct it, the fifth operation resulted in his distinctive "droopy eye" and reduced vision of about 50% on that side. He wore an eye patch during his first couple of years in school. "Tom is a delicate little guy, standing about 5'5"."

xref.title: Band Formation (1982)
xref.body: The core members, Tom York, Colin Greenwood, and Ed O'Brien, first met and started playing together in their final year at Abingdon, a private school in Oxford, around 1982. At this time, they were approximately 14 or 15 years old. Their initial setup included "three guitarists and a bad drum machine named Dr. Rhythm," and their very first gig was at a friend's birthday party. "Their first gig was at a friends birthday party. This would be sometime in 1982, which means everybody was about 14, 15 years old at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Recordings (1986)
xref.body: The earliest existing recording attributed to the band is a five-track cassette from 1986, which they self-issued at Abingdon. At this point, Johnny Greenwood was not yet a member, but a sax player named Razz Peterson was part of the lineup. The tape prominently featured 80s influences from bands like U2, Waterboys, Psychedelic Furs, and The Smiths, with Tom York handling lead vocals at 17 years old. "The earliest recording that seems to exist is a 1986 cassette that was recorded at Elbington."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Hiatus for College (1991)
xref.body: In 1991, "On a Friday" entered an extended hiatus as all five members pursued higher education at different universities. Ed O'Brien went to Manchester University, Colin Greenwood studied English literature at Cambridge, Phil Selway also studied English literature at Liverpool University, and Johnny Greenwood enrolled in both music and psychology programs at Oxford. Tom York decided to take a year off before attending university. "In 1997, a 1991 on a Friday went on an extended sort of hiatus."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Name Change to Radiohead (1991)
xref.body: After signing with EMI, the label expressed dissatisfaction with the name "On a Friday" and instructed the band to find a new one. Various suggestions were considered, including "Jude the Obscure" (deemed "too obscure" from the Thomas Hardy novel), "Music" (liked by Tom but rejected), and "Gravitates" (which "didn't have the right ring to it"). The definitive name, "Radiohead," was discovered when someone retrieved a 1986 Talking Heads album, "True Stories," from Tom York's DJ collection, which featured a song of the same name. The name change officially occurred at the end of 1991. "And so it came to pass that at the end of 1991, on a Friday, became known as Radiohead."

xref.title: Self-Leak Strategy for In Rainbows (2007)
xref.body: To counter unauthorized leaks and maintain artistic integrity, Radiohead secretly decided to "leak their own album" (In Rainbows) by releasing it directly to fans online through a pay-what-you-want model. This innovative approach allowed them to control the terms of release and bypass traditional distribution challenges. "As Tom York said to Wired Magazine, we are going to leak our own album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Thom Yorke's Personal Tragedy (2016)
xref.body: Thom Yorke and his partner, Rachel, separated after 16 years. A few months after the release of "A Moon-Shaped Pool" in December 2016, Rachel tragically died of cancer. "Another sad thing, Tom York and his partner Rachel separated after 16 years, and then she died of cancer that December, a few months after the album came out."

xref.title: Formation and Gigs
xref.body: The Headless Chickens were formed by Tom York, while he was at Exeter, and a bouncer named Shaq. The group was active in the city of Exeter, where they played "dozens of gigs." "he connected with a bouncer named Shaq, and they formed a group called The Headless Chickens, and they ended up playing dozens of gigs around the city of Exeter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Frustration with Music Leaks
xref.body: Radiohead was deeply annoyed by the pervasive issue of music leaks, especially in the internet era, where a single file from a hard drive could undermine meticulously planned marketing campaigns and result in significant lost revenue. Their last four albums, plus Thom Yorke's solo record, had all leaked prematurely, sometimes months in advance, prompting the band to consider a radical business model to prevent such occurrences. "In fact, the last four Radiohead albums, plus Tom York's solo record somehow made it into the wild before they were supposed to, sometimes weeks before, and sometimes months before, which really ticked them off."

xref.title: Influence on Tom Yorke
xref.body: During the recording sessions for "Okay Computer," Tom Yorke found himself "entranced with some old Johnny Cash records," indicating a musical influence or creative interest at the time. "Meanwhile Tom York found himself in trance with some old Johnny Cash records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for "Fake Plastic Trees"
xref.body: Legend suggests that Tom York's vocal performance on Radiohead's song "Fake Plastic Trees" was directly inspired by the late Jeff Buckley. Radiohead had reportedly seen Buckley perform at a local bar the night before recording the track. "legend has it that Tom's vocal performance on that track was inspired by the late Jeff Buckley, who in the band had seen at a local bar the night before."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Iron Lung Machine
xref.body: Tom York is rumored to possess a real iron lung machine at his home. "Tom apparently has a real one at home someplace."

xref.title: Twilight Soundtracks Contribution
xref.body: Paramore contributed to the various *Twilight* soundtracks that accompanied the film series. These soundtracks featured a nice selection of tunes, mostly album cuts and outtakes, from a range of artists spanning different genres. "The Paramore, Lincoln Park, Collective Soul, Death Cab for Cutie, Tom York, the Killers, Editors, Metric, Block Keys, Dead Weather, Beck, Vampire Weekend, Florence in the Machine."
